scenes.title: It guesses what comes next
scenes.narration: A GPT does one job. You give it some text, and it guesses what comes next.

steps.say: Here the text is: Once upon a time, in a land of math, there lived a.
It doesn't give one answer. It gives a chance for every possible next piece. Creature gets forty two percent.
Wizard and king get less. These numbers are made up, but the shape is the real thing.
Every other piece of text it knows shares what is left.

scenes.title: It adds one token at a time
scenes.narration: The model doesn't see words. It sees pieces called tokens.

steps.say: This sentence is fourteen of them.
Most common words are one token each, and the space in front of a word rides along with it.
The model picks one next token by its chance, say creature, and adds it to the end.
Then it runs again on the longer text to guess the next one. Token after token, a whole story comes out.

scenes.title: Six stops from text to chances
scenes.narration: Here is the whole trip from text to chances, in six stops.

steps.say: First the text is cut into tokens. A rare word gets split into smaller pieces.
Each token is swapped for a long list of numbers that stands for its meaning, looked up in a big table.
Then the tokens talk to each other. Model means something different after machine learning than after fashion.
Next, each token's numbers go through the same set of questions. These two stops take turns, again and again.
At the end, the last token's numbers are turned into a score for every token the model knows.
And one last step turns those scores into chances that add up to one hundred percent.

scenes.narration: A normal program follows rules a person wrote. A model like this is mostly numbers that were tuned.

steps.say: In a program, a person writes the rules. In a model, training nudges numbers called weights until the guesses get good.
Think of a line, y equals m x plus b. Training finds good values for m and b.
Now scale that up. GPT-3 has a hundred and seventy five billion of those numbers.
Once training is done, the weights stay fixed. Only your text changes from run to run.
Almost all the work is multiplying grids of weights by your text's numbers. Graphics chips are very good at that.

scenes.narration: Each token's list of numbers is a point in a huge space. GPT-3 uses 12,288 numbers per token.

steps.say: Words with close meanings end up close together. Near tower you find skyscraper, spire and lighthouse.
Directions mean something too. The step from man to woman is about the same as the step from king to queen.
Take sushi, add the step from Japan to Germany, and you land near bratwurst.
There's even a direction for plural, from cat to cats.
Multiply two lists number by number and add it all up. The total says how much they point the same way.

draw.write:
a · b is big when a and b
point the same way

scenes.narration: At first, a token's numbers only mean the word itself. As they pass through the layers, they soak up the text around them.

steps.say: Take the word king, in a play by Shakespeare. Before the first layer, king just means king.
A few layers in, it has picked up that this king rules Scotland.
Deeper still, it holds the story: he got the crown by murder.
By the last of GPT-3's ninety six layers, it even knows the style is old poetry.

scenes.narration: Here are a few of GPT-3's real sizes.

steps.say: Every token is a list of twelve thousand two hundred and eighty eight numbers.
It can look at two thousand and forty eight tokens at once. Anything earlier falls out of view.
The lookup table has one row for each of the 50,257 tokens it knows. That alone is over six hundred million weights.
All in, about a hundred and seventy five billion.

scenes.title: Softmax turns scores into chances
scenes.narration: Say the text is: Harry Potter's least favourite teacher, Professor. The model scores every possible next token.

steps.say: Here are six of those scores, and we'll pretend they're all there is. Banana gets minus three.
Raise e to each score. Now every number is above zero, and big scores pull far ahead.
Divide each by the total, 127.99. Now they add up to one hundred percent. Snape gets 52 percent.
The second row is only the start of Umbridge. The rest of her name would come on the next turns.

draw.note: only “Um”: the rest comes next turn

scenes.title: Temperature flattens or sharpens the chances
scenes.narration: There's a dial called temperature. Each score is divided by it before softmax.

steps.say: Turn it down near zero, and the top token takes almost everything. Snape gets 98 percent. The text is safe and repetitive.
At one, you get the plain softmax from before. Writing is fluent and still varied.
Turn it up to two, and the chances flatten out. Snape drops to 35 percent.
Push it much higher, and odd picks like banana start to get chosen, and the text turns to nonsense.

scenes.title: The whole trip, over and over
scenes.narration: Here is the whole map once more.

steps.say: Text becomes tokens, and each token becomes a list of numbers.
Attention and the MLP take turns, ninety six times in GPT-3.
Then the last list becomes scores, the scores become chances, and one token gets picked.
The pick joins the text, and it all runs again.
The part that does the most clever work is attention. How tokens ask each other questions is a story for another video.
